title: Weather Idiom Almanac
intro: A bolt from the blue, steal someone’s thunder, weather the storm. Pick the weather idiom that fits each situation.

A2.q: My neighbour walks the dog every morning, ___ .
A2.why: “Every morning” whatever the weather: “come rain or shine”.

A2.q: Ana is a real ___ — she makes everyone in class smile.
A2.why: She makes everyone smile, so she brightens the day: “a ray of sunshine”.

A2.q: I don't spend all my pension — I save some ___ .
A2.why: Saving money for hard times later: “for a rainy day”.

A2.q: I was ill last week, but now I feel as ___ .
A2.why: Ill last week, fine now: “as right as rain” means completely well again.

A2.q: He wanted to ask her to dance, but he got ___ at the last minute.
A2.why: He was nervous and didn’t do it at the last minute: he got “cold feet”.

A2.q: I can't come out tonight — I'm completely ___ with work.
A2.why: Too much work to go out: “snowed under” means buried in work.

A2.q: The crossword was ___ — I finished it in twenty minutes.
A2.why: Finished in twenty minutes, so it was very easy: “a breeze”.

A2.q: You'll be ___ if your wife finds out you broke her favourite mug.
A2.why: Your wife will be angry about the mug: you’ll be “in hot water”, in trouble.

A2.q: You've put salt in your coffee! You've had your ___ all morning.
A2.why: Salt in your coffee means you’re dreaming, not paying attention: your “head in the clouds”.

A2.q: As soon as I lost my job, he stopped calling — a real ___ .
A2.why: He was there in the good times and disappeared in the bad: “a fair-weather friend”.

A2.q: It's raining ___ — take an umbrella and a coat!
A2.why: “Take an umbrella” points to very heavy rain: “raining cats and dogs”.

A2.q: I can't come to class today — I'm feeling a bit ___ .
A2.why: Missing class because you feel a little ill: “under the weather”.

B1.q: I'd love to come tonight, but I'm exhausted — can I take ___ ?
B1.why: Saying no now but maybe another time: “take a rain check”.

B1.q: The company lost money all year, but somehow it managed to ___ .
B1.why: A hard year, but the company survived it: “weather the storm”.

B1.q: Everything is quiet now, but it feels like ___ — the grandchildren arrive for the summer on Monday.
B1.why: Quiet now, but a busy, noisy summer starts on Monday: “the calm before the storm”.

B1.q: Losing that job was hard, but every cloud has ___ — now I run my own business.
B1.why: Something good came out of losing the job: every cloud has “a silver lining”.

B1.q: It started as a discussion about money and turned into ___ .
B1.why: A discussion that got angry and loud became “a heated argument”.

B1.q: Ever since our argument, she's been giving me ___ .
B1.why: Since the argument she ignores me: “the cold shoulder”.

B1.q: I hadn't heard from Marta in years — then yesterday, ___ , she phoned me.
B1.why: No contact for years, then a sudden call: “out of the blue”.

B1.q: I've just retired, so please don't ___ by mentioning how small my pension is.
options: save it for a rainy day
B1.why: Spoiling someone’s happy moment with bad news: “rain on my parade”.

B1.q: Don't listen to his big promises — he's ___ .
B1.why: Big promises with nothing behind them: “full of hot air”.

B1.q: Your boss has warned you twice about being late — you're ___ .
B1.why: Two warnings already, so one more mistake could cost you: you’re “on thin ice”.

B1.q: Nobody spoke at the start of the meeting, so the doctor told a joke to ___ .
B1.why: Nobody spoke, so a joke started the conversation: “break the ice”.

B1.q: The sheriff could feel ___ the moment the stranger rode into town.
B1.why: The stranger means trouble is coming: “a storm brewing”.

B2.q: I was about to announce my engagement when my sister announced hers first — she completely ___ .
B2.why: She announced first and took my moment of attention: she “stole my thunder”.

B2.q: The news of his resignation came as ___ — nobody had suspected a thing.
B2.why: “Nobody had suspected a thing”, so a total shock: “a bolt from the blue”.

B2.q: Her first novel took the literary world ___ .
B2.why: A huge, fast success with everyone: “took the world by storm”.

B2.q: Somehow the journalists ___ of the merger before it was announced.
B2.why: They heard about the secret before the announcement: “got wind of” it.

B2.q: He ___ , quit his job, and bought a one-way ticket to Buenos Aires.
options: took the wind out of his sails
B2.why: Quitting and leaving on a one-way ticket is very risky: “threw caution to the wind”.

B2.q: The boss walked in with ___ — someone was clearly in trouble.
B2.why: “Someone was clearly in trouble”: an angry look is “a face like thunder”.

B2.q: Stop ___ — you're forty, you're never going to be a rock star.
B2.why: A dream that will never come true: “chasing rainbows”.

B2.q: Tourist season only lasts three months here, so local businesses have to make hay ___ .
B2.why: Only three good months, so use them: “make hay while the sun shines”.

B2.q: His new colleagues barely spoke to him at lunch — ___ indeed.
B2.why: They barely spoke to him: a cold, unfriendly welcome is “a frosty reception”.

B2.q: After the scandal, his former allies left him ___ .
B2.why: His allies abandoned him: “left out in the cold”.

B2.q: Everyone in Ruzafa was furious about the new parking rules, but it was ___ — by Friday nobody cared.
B2.why: Everyone was angry, then nobody cared: a fuss about nothing is “a storm in a teacup”.

B2.q: When their first grandchild was born at La Fe hospital, they were ___ .
options: in the eye of the storm
B2.why: A first grandchild brings huge happiness: “on cloud nine”.

C1.q: First the car broke down, then the boiler, then the roof — it never rains but it ___ .
C1.why: Problem after problem: “it never rains but it pours”.

C1.q: She had prepared a triumphant speech, but the early press leak rather ___ .
options: took the wind out of her sails
C1.why: The leak spoilt her triumph and confidence: “took the wind out of her sails”.

C1.q: Declaring that income as 'a gift' to avoid tax is ___ , even if it's technically legal.
C1.why: “Technically legal” but almost wrong: “sailing close to the wind”.

C1.q: The hostel was noisy and cramped, but it was 2 a.m. and we were exhausted — ___ .
C1.why: Noisy and cramped, but any shelter will do when you’re desperate: “any port in a storm”.

C1.q: I will have the kitchen finished by Friday, ___ .
C1.why: A firm promise whatever happens: “come hell or high water”.

C1.q: Since the fraud investigation began, the director has been ___ at work.
C1.why: An investigation means suspicion hangs over him: “under a cloud”.

C1.q: The inheritance from a great-aunt she'd never met was quite ___ .
C1.why: Money from a great-aunt she never met is an unexpected gift: “a windfall”.

C1.q: The factory closure was devastating, but the demolition firm did well out of it — it's an ill wind that blows nobody ___ .
C1.why: Bad news for some is good for others: “an ill wind that blows nobody any good”.

C1.q: The team looked exhausted at half-time, but they got ___ and scored three goals.
C1.why: Tired at half-time, then fresh energy and three goals: “a second wind”.

C1.q: As the minister at the centre of the leak inquiry, she has spent the week in ___ .
C1.why: She is at the centre of the trouble: “the eye of the storm”.

C1.q: Before choosing a side in the debate, the MP waited to see ___ .
options: which way the wind was blowing
whether it was raining cats and dogs
C1.why: The MP waited to see what most people thought: “which way the wind was blowing”.

C1.q: The rancher's daughter married the travelling doctor after only three weeks: a real ___ .
C1.why: Married after three weeks: a fast, exciting love affair is “a whirlwind romance”.
